sources.citation: He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition, CVPR 2016
sources.passage: Increasing the depth of a conventional convolutional network can increase training error, even though the added layers could in principle implement identity mappings. A residual block instead learns a residual function F(x) and adds the input through a shortcut, producing F(x) + x. Identity shortcuts add no parameters when dimensions match; learned projections can reconcile dimension changes. This parameterization makes an identity mapping easier to represent and enabled substantially deeper networks to be optimized.
sources.technical_summary: ResNet mitigates degradation by parameterizing blocks as F(x) + x rather than learning H(x) directly. Identity shortcuts ease optimization without extra parameters, while projection shortcuts handle dimension changes, enabling substantially deeper CNNs.
sources.accessible_summary: ResNet makes deeper image models easier to optimize by letting each block learn only a change to its input, then adding the original input back. Adjusted shortcuts are used when the representations have different sizes.

sources.citation: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, NeurIPS 2017
sources.passage: The Transformer replaces recurrence and convolution with attention mechanisms. Encoder layers combine multi-head self-attention with position-wise feed-forward networks. Decoder layers also attend to encoder outputs and mask future positions. Scaled dot-product attention compares queries with keys, applies a softmax, and uses the weights to combine values. Multiple heads operate in different learned subspaces. Because there is no recurrence, positional information is added separately and training can be parallelized across sequence positions.
sources.technical_summary: The Transformer replaces recurrence with multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers. Scaled query-key attention mixes value vectors; positional encodings supply order and causal masks prevent decoder access to future tokens.
sources.accessible_summary: The Transformer handles a sequence by letting each token weigh information from other tokens instead of processing them strictly one at a time. It separately records order and hides future tokens during generation, allowing parallel training.

sources.citation: Ronneberger et al., U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation, MICCAI 2015
sources.passage: U-Net is a convolutional architecture for dense image segmentation. Its contracting path repeatedly applies convolutions and downsampling to capture context. A symmetric expanding path upsamples feature maps to recover spatial resolution. At each scale, feature maps from the contracting path are concatenated with the corresponding expanding-path features. These skip connections restore fine spatial information that would otherwise be lost during downsampling, allowing precise localization even when only a limited number of annotated biomedical images are available.
sources.technical_summary: U-Net couples a convolutional encoder with a symmetric upsampling decoder for dense segmentation. Cross-scale skip concatenations restore high-resolution encoder features, combining contextual representations with precise localization under limited labelled data.
sources.accessible_summary: U-Net labels each part of an image by first shrinking the image representation to understand context and then expanding it to recover detail. Shortcuts copy fine information from each shrinking stage to the matching expanding stage.

sources.passage: Ordinary kriging predicts a spatial variable at an unobserved location using a weighted combination of nearby observations. The weights are obtained from a fitted variogram or covariance model and constrained to sum to one, giving an unbiased linear predictor when the unknown mean is locally constant. Observations are not weighted by distance alone: their spatial covariance and redundancy with one another also matter. The same model yields a kriging variance that quantifies uncertainty induced by the sampling geometry and assumed spatial dependence.
sources.technical_summary: Ordinary kriging is a best linear unbiased predictor under an unknown constant mean. Variogram-derived covariance determines weights subject to a unit-sum constraint, accounting for inter-sample redundancy and yielding a model-based kriging variance.
sources.accessible_summary: Ordinary kriging estimates a value at an unmeasured location by combining nearby measurements. It considers both proximity and how measurements vary together, avoids counting redundant observations twice, and reports uncertainty based on the sampling pattern.

sources.citation: Devlin et al., BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding, NAACL 2019
sources.passage: BERT pre-trains a Transformer encoder on unlabeled text so that every layer can use both left and right context. Its masked-language-model objective replaces or obscures selected input tokens and trains the network to recover them from the surrounding sequence. The original model also uses a next-sentence-prediction objective over pairs of text segments. After pre-training, the same encoder can be fine-tuned for tasks such as question answering and natural-language inference with only a small task-specific output layer.
sources.technical_summary: BERT pre-trains a deeply bidirectional Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and, in the original formulation, next-sentence prediction. Fine-tuning adds a small task head while updating the shared contextual representations end to end.
sources.accessible_summary: BERT first learns from unlabeled text by hiding some words and predicting them using context on both sides. The resulting model can then be adapted to tasks such as question answering by adding a small output component and training on task examples.

sources.citation: Kipf and Welling, Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks, ICLR 2017
sources.passage: A graph convolutional network updates node representations by mixing each node's features with features from its neighbors. Kipf and Welling derive a simple propagation rule from a localized first-order approximation to spectral graph convolution. Adding self-connections and normalizing by node degrees stabilizes this aggregation. Stacking layers lets supervision from a small labeled subset shape representations that incorporate both node attributes and local graph structure, with computation scaling linearly in the number of edges.
sources.technical_summary: The GCN uses a renormalized first-order spectral propagation rule to aggregate self and neighbor features. Stacked message-passing layers support semi-supervised node classification by combining attributes with local topology at cost linear in the edge count.
sources.accessible_summary: A GCN represents each graph node by repeatedly combining its own information with information from connected neighbors. This allows labels available for only some nodes to guide predictions elsewhere while keeping computation efficient on sparse graphs.

sources.citation: Ho et al., Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, NeurIPS 2020
sources.passage: A denoising diffusion probabilistic model defines a forward Markov process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to data according to a variance schedule. A neural network learns the reverse transitions, commonly by predicting the noise present at a randomly selected timestep. To generate a sample, the model starts from Gaussian noise and repeatedly applies the learned denoising transitions. The training objective is connected to a variational bound and to denoising score matching.
sources.technical_summary: A DDPM fixes a Gaussian forward noising chain and learns its parameterized reverse process, typically through timestep-conditioned noise prediction. Sampling iteratively denoises from the Gaussian prior; the objective relates a variational bound to denoising score matching.
sources.accessible_summary: A diffusion model learns to reverse a process that slowly corrupts training examples with random noise. It creates new examples by starting with noise and removing it over many steps, using a network trained to estimate the corruption at each stage.

sources.citation: Chen and Guestrin, XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System, KDD 2016
sources.passage: Gradient tree boosting builds an additive predictor by fitting each new decision tree to improve the current ensemble under a differentiable loss. XGBoost uses a regularized objective and a second-order approximation involving gradients and Hessians to score candidate tree structures and leaf weights. Its sparsity-aware split algorithm assigns a learned default direction to missing values. A weighted quantile sketch supports approximate split finding, while cache-aware and out-of-core system designs make training scalable.
sources.technical_summary: XGBoost performs regularized additive tree boosting with second-order gradient statistics for split and leaf scoring. Sparsity-aware default directions, weighted quantile sketches, and cache-aware out-of-core execution provide scalable approximate tree construction.
sources.accessible_summary: XGBoost builds a strong predictor by adding decision trees one at a time, with each tree correcting the current ensemble. It controls tree complexity and uses specialized methods for missing values, approximate splits, and efficient processing of large datasets.
